events.description: Amin deposed and executed in a coup the cable says was planned and executed by the Soviet Union.
Massive Soviet airlift of troops and materiel into Kabul during the two days before the coup, with over 100 flights (figure partly illegible).
Soviet and Afghan troops fought for control of Radio Afghanistan; three Afghan tanks were destroyed and Soviet troops took Afghan prisoners.
Hours of fighting near Darulaman Palace, Amin's residence.
Radio announcements, apparently from Soviet transmitters, said Babrak Karmal had succeeded Amin as President of the Revolutionary Council.

After the April coup (the text reads '1976', apparently an OCR or typographical error), Babrak was made deputy prime minister, then within months 'exiled' as ambassador to Prague, a post held about six weeks.
At least the equivalent of a Soviet combat regiment arrived at Bagram Air Force Base; five or more Soviet divisions were massed north of the border.
The new regime made conciliatory announcements and offered to negotiate with the insurgent groups.
Hafizullah Amin deposed and executed in a Soviet-planned coup; Babrak Karmal installed.
Massive Soviet airlift of troops and materiel into Kabul in the two days before the coup.
Soviet troops fought Afghan troops for control of Radio Afghanistan; tanks near the radio building destroyed.
Prerecorded announcements broadcast from Soviet transmitters announced Babrak as president of the Revolutionary Council.
After the April 1978 coup Babrak became Deputy Prime Minister, then was exiled as ambassador to Prague.
A Soviet combat regiment equivalent arrived at Bagram as the airlift continued.

key_claims: The US assessed that the 27 December 1979 coup that deposed and executed Hafizullah Amin was clearly planned and executed by the Soviet Union.
The first announcements of the coup apparently came from Soviet transmitters, and were pre-recorded and repeated on several frequencies.
Babrak Karmal was installed by the Soviets and will be dependent on Moscow for his survival.
The scale of the Soviet buildup, including five or more divisions north of the border, suggests military objectives beyond a change of government in Kabul.
Most insurgents are expected to reject Babrak's overtures because they will see him as even more a creature of the Soviet Union than Amin.
The Afghan Army is demoralized and may suffer further desertions, and the Soviets will face difficulty rebuilding it and combating the widespread insurgency.
